claims.text: As-synthesized equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC alloy.
Equal-atomic NbMoTaW has poor room-temperature ductility.
Adding approximately 2 at.% Zr to equal-atomic NbMoTaW will improve room-temperature ductility.
The ductility improvement from Zr addition will result from reduced grain-boundary embrittlement.
Approximately 2 at.% Zr will segregate to NbMoTaW grain boundaries during cooling after homogenization.
Grain-boundary Zr segregation will reduce local stress concentrations.
Grain-boundary Zr segregation will facilitate dislocation nucleation and motion.
A homogenization anneal near 1600 °C will ensure complete Zr solubility and a homogeneous single-phase BCC state.
Controlled cooling can permit beneficial Zr grain-boundary segregation without producing secondary phases.
The Zr-modified alloy will show improved room-temperature tensile and bending ductility through enhanced grain-boundary plasticity.
Adding approximately 2 at.% Zr will leave 1600 °C mechanical performance comparable to or slightly better than that of untreated NbMoTaW.
High-temperature homogenization will nullify the localized mechanical effects of Zr.
The high-temperature strength of the modified alloy is governed predominantly by the bulk matrix.
Adding approximately 2 at.% Zr will leave irradiation resistance unchanged relative to untreated NbMoTaW.
The irradiation resistance of the modified alloy is governed predominantly by the bulk matrix.
The Zr-modified alloy will exhibit defect recombination and irradiation-damage tolerance similar to untreated NbMoTaW.
The beneficial effect of Zr is confined to a narrow composition window near 2 at.%.
Excessive Zr may produce deleterious secondary phases or segregation.
Secondary phases or excessive segregation caused by higher Zr content could compromise room-temperature ductility and high-temperature performance.
